"We took BrickLink offline after identifying unusual activity on the platform," the website states. "Our immediate priority was to secure the site, protect our members and ensure the integrity of BrickLink. "Before bringing the site back online, we need to fully understand what has happened. events.excerpt: Nvidia CEO and founder Jensen Huang has been ousted after nearly two weeks of controversy that, at times, felt more like a soap opera than reality: a wealthy businessman, reported affairs, and an alleged Chinese spy and GPU smuggler. For Nvidia’s board, it seems there was no question Huang had to go. The man behind what was recently the most valuable company in the world proved too big a liability to retain in any capacity. He was too toxic even for a demotion from CEO to chairman, a vantage point that would have retained Huang as the face of the company even if he could no longer be trusted to run it. Replacing him won’t be so easy. Nvidia now faces an identity crisis. Huang, who has led the company for more than three decades, has no clear successor. The GPU slinger has no shortage of brilliant engineers, but executives capable of wrangling one of the biggest and most influential brands in the world, not so much. Ian Buck, father of CUDA and Nvidia’s VP of hyperscale and HPC is currently favored by many to be Huang’s successor. Buck has taken on a more public role within Nvidia in recent years headlining keynotes at events like Supercomputing and the AI Infra Summit. events.excerpt: Drone and missile strikes have inflicted unprecedented damage on data centers in Eastern Europe and the Middle East this year, disrupting cloud services for millions of people and permanently deleting some Amazon Web Services customer data. To explore what this all means for modern society’s reliance on cloud resilience, I will be hosting a live conversation titled "Drone attacks and data centers: New Risks for Big Tech" on Tuesday, November 17 at 1 pm ET with Joseph Jarnecki , a senior research fellow at the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI), a UK defense and security think tank. He leads RUSI’s work on how cloud services factor into national security and defense, along with tech sovereignty efforts. Jarnecki has done extensive research on how Ukraine strengthened its cloud resilience with Western partners despite facing both cyberattacks and kinetic attacks at the start of the full-scale Russian invasion, and explored what that means for NATO and European governments’ cloud adoption plans. events.excerpt: A Zcash governance trilogy, part 3 of 3. Or navigating the dark forest without turning on all the lights TL;DR: In a private system we cannot know who holds voting power, how many people sit behind it, or whom they are connected to. The answer is not to abolish the privacy. It is to bound what any vote can decide, so that capturing one voting mechanism cannot confer control over the whole system. Part 1 : An Ode to Rough Consensus . Part 2 : When We Disagree: Making Rough Consensus Work . Part 3 : Governance in a Shielded World. Zcash is building a parallel financial system, outside of but adjacent to the existing one. Its governance, however, remains entirely inside human institutions. That private financial system starts from a different assumption from the one we have become accustomed to elsewhere: privacy is normal. In such a system, private by default should be the ordinary situation, not a special mode for people with something to hide. Traditional finance already runs part of its markets this way. Dark pools let large investors trade without displaying their orders, so that others cannot trade against them. Dark does not mean lawless. events.excerpt: Google is continuing its elemental AI naming scheme with the new Gemini 4 Hydrogen . These names are less descriptive than the Pro/Flash monikers of earlier releases, but Hydrogen's purpose is clear: It replaces the faster, more economical Flash models most people in Google's ecosystem use. With Google's recent Argon and Carbon releases, the rollout was staged and began with cybersecurity researchers. Even when general availability began, Google restricted access to users paying for its most expensive AI subscription. The limits for Hydrogen are much more relaxed, with access beginning immediately. This model has replaced Gemini 3.8 Flash across the company's products. Google claims that Hydrogen represents a major improvement versus the previous Flash model. It runs in one of four thinking levels (low, medium, high, and the new xhigh), and even in high mode, it's 2.5 times faster than Flash 3.8. Plus, it reduces "fabricated claims" by more than 5x, according to Google's analysis. Users will also see gains in code generation, with Hydrogen more than tripling 3.8 Flash's score in Terminal-Bench. In some cases, Hydrogen even trades blows with Argon. It managed a score of 54 in the popular Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index with xhigh mode versus 50 for Argon. Read full article
events.headline: Google rolls out Gemini 4 Hydrogen, finally replacing 3.8 Flash

events.excerpt: This Node and Miner patch release is recommended for all node operators and storage providers. It moves the FVM to wasmtime 48 LTS for performance and security improvements, fixes CreateBackup path containment, and makes Ethereum JSON-RPC quantity validation stricter. Review the upgrade warning before upgrading. ✨ Notable Changes ⚠️ Upgrade warning: Ethereum JSON-RPC rejects negative, unprefixed, leading-zero and oversized (>256-bit) big integers. Use canonical 0x encoding ( 0x0 for zero). The Go helper api.NewErrNegativeGasPrice is removed. ( #13938 ) The FVM now runs on wasmtime 48 LTS for every network version, via ref-fvm v4.9.0 . Security: wasmtime 48 is a long-term-support release that gets security fixes until ~August 2028. Performance: on a mainnet node over 24 hours, median execution time per unit of gas fell about 18% for messages and 11% overall, with no regressions seen on mainnet or calibnet ( measurements ). ( #14023 ) 📝 All Changes Node: Changes since v1.39.0 Miner: Changes since miner/v1.39.0 All PRs (9) Fixes fix(api): reject CreateBackup paths outside LOTUS_BACKUP_BASE_PATH ( #14020 ) fix(eth)!: reject non-canonical and oversized JSON quantities ( #13938 ) Chores and other build: update Lotus Node and Miner version to v1.39.1-dev in master ( #14010 ) chore(deps)

events.excerpt: eMudhra's private key exposure has been a security disaster, but it also means that you can block those annoying ads on smart TVs if you’re so inclined. Luckily for those with some know-how and a hatred of smart TV ads, Czech software developer Daniel Vrátil has done the work for you and published his project on GitHub for anyone who wants to take a stab at it - and do the legwork to add support for their own ad-riddled television. Vrátil said he’d been blocking ads on his Samsung smart TV using a Pi-hole (DNS-based ad-blocking software that can run on a Raspberry Pi, for those unfamiliar), but right around the time the eMudhra certificate leak mess unfolded, he had messed something up while tinkering with his home lab and the ads were back. First, here's a bit of background on the eMudhra mess. The company, based in India, operated a publicly trusted HTTPS certificate authority and says it has issued more than 60 million digital certificates. The gap was also wider across the last 30 days, with Midnight completing 1,487,836 transactions while just 308,050 were processed on Zcash. Charles Hoskinson, the founder of Cardano and a leading figure behind Midnight, was suitably impressed, taking to X with a short message: “Midnight is growing. Private Smart contracts are the future.” The outperformance didn’t end on transaction counts alone, with the native tokens of the two privacy-preserving platforms, NIGHT and ZEC, moving in very different directions. At the time of writing, data from CoinGecko showed NIGHT near $0.047, an uptick of more than 9% in 24 hours. events.excerpt: Description A few small nit cleanups on the synchronizer component in consensus. Behavior change: fetch_blocks_from_peers now returns as soon as no request is in flight, instead of idling until the 4s FETCH_FROM_PEERS_TIMEOUT. This affects two cases: no request was sent because every selected block was already locked, or the last outstanding request failed with no peer left to retry on. In both cases no further network request is sent, and a failed request still waits the full 2s request timeout, so periodic runs cannot repeat faster than every ~2s on failures. The only new cost is local: while all selected blocks are locked, the scheduler polls get_missing_blocks at its default 200ms cadence instead of every 4s, which is the same cadence it already uses during fast successful sync. Added a test covering both cases. Test plan CI/PT Release notes Check each box that your changes affect. If none of the boxes relate to your changes, release notes aren't required. For each box you select, include information after the relevant heading that describes the impact of your changes that a user might notice and any actions they must take to implement updates. Protocol: Nodes (Validators and Full nodes): gRPC: JSON-RPC: GraphQL: CLI: Rust SDK: Indexing Framework: Co-authored-by: Claude Fable

events.excerpt: Printing with Windows has always been something of a choose-your-own-adventure, and November's security update has added another unwelcome plot twist: documents containing certain images might not print. The issue affects images rendered with a height or width of zero at the selected printing resolution. These might not be visible to users, but can form part of a document's watermarking or layout. After the update, those invisible objects can apparently make the printed document disappear too. Microsoft said: "The issue was observed when printing Microsoft Word documents using the Windows Graphics Device Interface (GDI), but printing from other applications might also be affected." According to the notification (WI1549472), most versions of Windows are affected, from the latest Windows 11 26H2 through Windows 10 Enterprise LTSC 2016. Windows Server from 2025 to 2016 is also affected. Users need not have added these objects themselves. Microsoft says document-generation tools can insert them even when no graphic is visible. events.excerpt: A Democratic takeover of Congress may look like bad news for the industry, but Bitwise Chief Investment Officer Matt Hougan believes the bigger picture tells a different story. While the election could bring short-term market volatility, Hougan said that the changing demographics of Congress matter more to crypto’s long-term prospects than which party holds power. Importance of Demographics The latest election put Democrats in control of both houses of Congress, with Elizabeth Warren likely to become chair of the Senate Banking Committee. Given her history of opposing crypto, the development has raised concerns about what could come next for the industry. Hougan, however, does not see the election as a major setback. According to the lobbying group Stand With Crypto, the incoming Senate has 51 pro-crypto members, compared with 52 in the outgoing Congress. In the House, at least 241 members have received an A or B rating on crypto policy, which gives them a solid majority in the 425-member caucus. The more interesting change is the age of the lawmakers entering Congress, according to Hougan. Incoming senators are, on average, 14 years younger than those leaving. events.excerpt: This release contains bugfixes and improvements to the stacks-node and stacks-signer binaries, ensuring more consistent block production. This release is compatible with chainstate directories from 4.0.x. This release is recommended for all Stacks node and signer operators. This release includes the following changes: https://github.com/stacks-network/stacks-core/blob/4.0.6/CHANGELOG.md ⚠️ Breaking Changes Unused speculative tries from mining and block-proposal validation are no longer persisted. MARF databases automatically migrate to schema 4 on writable open, removing the legacy mined_blocks table and its stored tries. Older binaries cannot open upgraded databases, including in read-only mode; upgrade chainstate inspection and snapshot tooling alongside the node. Signers in this release rely on the node's new GET /v3/blocks/:block_id/view endpoint and the canonical field on /v3/sortitions to release a signed block that a Bitcoin fork has orphaned. Against an older node a signer stays safe but never releases such a block, which can stall a tenure after a reorg. Upgrade the stacks-node before, or together with, its signer. Removed the stackslib::chainstate::stacks::index module; the MARF now lives in the stacks-marf crate. Downstream library consumers should import from stacks_m
events.headline: Release 4.0.6
